\equiv B \land (L \lor \neg L)



One of L and \neg L always holds:

\equiv B \land \text{true} \equiv B



The lab-open condition has canceled from the policy. Ask whether that was intended. The identity used is (X and Y) or (X and Z) equivalent to X and (Y or Z). The law of excluded middle makes L or not L true under every classical assignment. Rewriting exposes redundancies, but does not decide whether a requirement is appropriate.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
A Small Toolbox for Rewriting







Law
Equivalence




Double negation
\neg\neg P \equiv P


Identity
P \land \text{true} \equiv P; P \lor \text{false} \equiv P


Domination
P \lor \text{true} \equiv \text{true}; P \land \text{false} \equiv \text{false}


Idempotence
P \land P \equiv P; P \lor P \equiv P


Implication
(P \rightarrow Q) \equiv \neg P \lor Q




Rewrite \neg(P \rightarrow Q) without an implication.


\neg(\neg P \lor Q) \equiv P \land \neg Q: precisely the case that violates the implication.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
section: Mini-Lab: Does This Policy Say Enough?
text:
Mini-Lab: Does This Policy Say Enough?
B = valid badge; V = approved visitor; E = emergency; D = unlock.
The intended policy: unlock exactly when authorized and no emergency is active.
The proposed rules are:

((B \lor V) \land \neg E) \rightarrow D
 
D \rightarrow \neg E


Could both rules be true while an unauthorized person gets in? Find an assignment or explain why not.


Allow three minutes in pairs. Suggested prompts: what happens if both B and V are false? What does the second rule actually require? Do not assume that a proposition is false just because no rule requires it to be true. The rules constrain possible access decisions; they are not a sequential program with an implicit else branch.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
section: A Missing Direction Leaves a Gap
text:
A Missing Direction Leaves a Gap
Try an unauthorized person, no emergency, and an unlocked door:

B=\text{false},\quad V=\text{false},\quad
E=\text{false},\quad D=\text{true}








Proposed rule
Evaluation




((B \lor V) \land \neg E) \rightarrow D
\text{false} \rightarrow \text{true}: true


D \rightarrow \neg E
\text{true} \rightarrow \text{true}: true




Missing requirement: unlocking must require authorization.

D \rightarrow (B \lor V)



All written rules can be satisfied while the intended policy is violated.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
section: Repair the Policy with Both Directions
text:
Repair the Policy with Both Directions

D \leftrightarrow ((B \lor V) \land \neg E)


Authorization and no emergency guarantee unlocking.
Unlocking requires authorization and no emergency.


What must D be in each case?

Valid badge, emergency active.
Approved visitor, no badge, no emergency.
No badge, no visitor approval, no emergency.



False; true; false. The two directions now specify the complete Boolean decision.


Give students one minute, then reveal. The repaired biconditional is equivalent to all three implications from the preceding slides. It is complete only for this simplified Boolean authorization decision; real systems require additional details such as identity, timing, access rights, failure handling, and safety requirements. The activity demonstrates specification debugging, not deployment-ready access control.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
What Propositional Logic Leaves Out







Need
What changes?




Facts about many people
First-order logic adds objects and predicates


“Every approved visitor has a host”
Quantifiers express general rules


“The door eventually locks”
Temporal logic expresses time relationships


A sensor is only 90% reliable
A probabilistic model represents uncertainty




Choose the representation for the task. Today, each atom is a fixed true-or-false statement.


This replaces the old broad types-of-logic survey with a motivation for richer representations. Explain the distinction between truth values and an agent’s uncertain beliefs. No quantifier exercises here; First-Order Logic comes after Propositional Inference. Probability is a separate later part of the course.
[Sources] - AIMA, Russell and Norvig: propositional logic, first-order logic, and probabilistic reasoning. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Takeaways



Atoms: define one stable statement per symbol.
Connectives: distinguish OR, XOR, implication, and iff.
Translation: check “only if,” “unless,” and negation scope.
Truth tables: evaluate every assignment systematically.
Equivalence: preserve truth values when rewriting.





A formula says exactly what its truth conditions allow, not everything its author intended.

Asset credits

Close the opening badge question. Students should now be able to give the missing reverse implication and a concrete assignment that exposes the gap. Next lecture asks what conclusions must hold across every world compatible with a collection of formulas.
[Sources] - Public-domain OpenClipart brain/lightbulb: https://openclipart.org/detail/266221/brain-light-bulb. [/Sources]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Transformers, Continued
Today: multi-head attention, decoding, causal training, positional encodings, transformer blocks, and transformers beyond language.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Recall: Scaled Dot-Product Attention

\operatorname{Attention}(Q,K,V)
=
V\cdot \operatorname{softmax}\left(\frac{K^TQ}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)




Term
Meaning




K^TQ
similarity scores


\operatorname{softmax}
converts scores into weights


V
content being mixed


\sqrt{d_k}
stabilizing scale

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Multi-Head Attention
Instead of one attention head, use many heads with different projections.




Different heads can attend to different relationships in the same sequence.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Multi-Head Formula

\operatorname{MultiHead}(\mathcal{W},X,X_Q)
=
W_O
\begin{bmatrix}
\operatorname{Attn}(W_{K,1},W_{Q,1},W_{V,1},X,X_Q)\\
\operatorname{Attn}(W_{K,2},W_{Q,2},W_{V,2},X,X_Q)\\
\vdots\\
\operatorname{Attn}(W_{K,m},W_{Q,m},W_{V,m},X,X_Q)
\end{bmatrix}

The output projection W_O brings the concatenated heads back to the desired embedding dimension.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Self-Attention
Self-attention means the sequence attends to itself:

X_Q=X

In autoregressive language modeling:

Each position builds a latent representation.
It should use previous context.
It should not see future tokens.


That last condition is why we need causal masking.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Inference: Next Token
Given a hidden representation h:

h=\operatorname{MultiHead}(\mathcal{W},X,x_n)

Predict the next-token distribution:

\operatorname{softmax}(B^Th)

where B contains token embeddings for the vocabulary.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Temperature Sampling
Logits \ell_i become probabilities through a temperature-scaled softmax:

p_i=
\frac{\exp(\ell_i/T)}
{\sum_j \exp(\ell_j/T)}




Temperature
Effect




low T
sharper, more deterministic


T=1
ordinary softmax


high T
flatter, more diverse




Temperature changes only the sampling distribution, not the model weights.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Top-K Sampling
Full-vocabulary sampling includes a long tail of tiny probabilities.
Top-K keeps only the K most likely tokens:

\tilde{s}_i=
\begin{cases}
s_i, & \text{if } i \text{ is among the top-}K \text{ logits},\\
-\infty, & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}


Temperature controls sharpness; top-K controls which candidate tokens are even allowed.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Training by Next-Token Prediction
Sentence:



token 0
token 1
token 2
token 3
token 4
token 5




<start>
Attention
is
all
you
need



Training examples:



Prefix
Query token
Target next token




<start>
<start>
Attention


<start> Attention
Attention
is


<start> Attention is
is
all


<start> Attention is all
all
you

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Causal Masking
Rather than slicing every prefix separately, train all positions at once with a mask.


scores = KTQ / sqrt(d_k)


for each query position i


for each key position j


if j > i: scores[j, i] = -infinity


weights = softmax(scores)

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Causal Mask Matrix
Future positions receive -\infty before softmax.




Each token can attend only to itself and earlier tokens.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Layer Normalization
Layer normalization stabilizes training.
For embedding x\in\mathbb{R}^{d_e}:

y=
\frac{x-\mathbb{E}[x]}
{\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}[x]+\epsilon}}
\gamma+\beta

where \gamma and \beta are trainable scale and shift parameters.

Normalization keeps intermediate activations in a better numerical range.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Attention Is Permutation-Invariant
For any permutation matrix P:

\operatorname{Attn}(W_K,W_Q,W_V,XP,X_Q)
=
\operatorname{Attn}(W_K,W_Q,W_V,X,X_Q)

Meaning: attention over a set of key/value tokens has no built-in notion of order.

five minus two and two minus five contain similar words, but order changes the meaning.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Positional Encoding
Add a position-dependent vector to each token embedding:

\text{embedding}(x_i,i)
=
\text{token encoding}(x_i)
+
\text{positional encoding}(i)

Sinusoidal positional encoding:

[\operatorname{PE}(t)]_j=
\begin{cases}
\sin\left(\frac{t}{10000^{2k/d_e}}\right),&\text{if } j=2k,\\
\cos\left(\frac{t}{10000^{2k/d_e}}\right),&\text{if } j=2k+1.
\end{cases}

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Sinusoidal Intuition
A sine wave has frequency and phase:

x(t)=a\sin(2\pi ft+\phi)




Different dimensions use different frequencies, so the model receives both local and long-range position signals.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI

CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Rotary Positional Embedding (RoPE)
RoPE applies position information inside attention by rotating query and key vectors.

R_\theta(i)=
\begin{bmatrix}
\cos(i\theta)&-\sin(i\theta)\\
\sin(i\theta)&\cos(i\theta)
\end{bmatrix}


\tilde{q}_i=R_\theta(i)q_i,\qquad
\tilde{k}_j=R_\theta(j)k_j


Many modern LLMs use RoPE because attention scores can encode relative position differences.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
RoPE Relative Position
Using rotation identities:

\langle \tilde{q}_i,\tilde{k}_j\rangle
=
\langle q_i,R_\theta(j-i)k_j\rangle

Result:

The dot product depends on the offset (j-i).
Relative position enters the attention score directly.
This helps long-context extrapolation and relative reasoning.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Transformer Block Overview
A transformer block combines:

Multi-head self-attention (MHSA).
Feed-forward network (FFN).
Residual connections.
Layer normalization.


Residuals let each layer learn a refinement instead of relearning the entire representation.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text: Transformer Block Diagram

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Pre-LN vs. Post-LN
Pre-LN (common in modern deep transformers)

x+\operatorname{MHSA}(\operatorname{LN}(x))
\rightarrow
x+\operatorname{FFN}(\operatorname{LN}(x))

Post-LN (original Transformer style)

\operatorname{LN}(x+\operatorname{MHSA}(x))
\rightarrow
\operatorname{LN}(x+\operatorname{FFN}(x))


Pre-LN is usually easier to optimize for very deep models.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Key-Value (KV) Cache
During autoregressive generation, tokens are produced one at a time.
Without caching, the model recomputes keys and values for all previous tokens at every step.




KV cache is one reason deployed LLM inference can be fast enough for interactive use.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Prompt Engineering
Prompt engineering is the practice of designing inputs to guide LLM outputs.
Useful habits:

Be explicit about the task.
Provide structure or templates.
Include examples when format matters.
Restrict ambiguity.
Iterate and refine.


Instead of Explain Transformers, try Explain Transformers in 3 bullet points suitable for a first-year CS student.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Types of Prompting







Type
Idea




zero-shot
no examples, only an instruction


few-shot
show input-output examples


chain-of-thought style
ask for step-by-step reasoning when appropriate


system/instruction design
set high-level behavior, role, or constraints


structured output
require JSON, tables, bullets, or schemas

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Evaluating Language Models
Perplexity measures how well a model predicts a ground-truth sequence:

\operatorname{Perplexity}
=
\exp\left(
-\frac{1}{N}
\sum_{i=1}^N
\log p(w_i\mid w_{<i})
\right)

Other common text metrics:

BLEU: precision-oriented n-gram overlap, common in translation.
ROUGE: recall-oriented overlap, common in summarization.


Metrics are useful, but they rarely capture everything humans care about.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Transformers Beyond Language
Transformers are not just for text.
They can be applied whenever data can be represented as a sequence of tokens:

image patches,
audio frames,
video tokens,
graph or trajectory tokens,
multimodal inputs.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Vision Transformers (ViT)
Vision Transformer (ViT) treats an image as a sequence of patches.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Linear Patch Encoding
For an image x\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times C}:

Split into N fixed-size patches.
Flatten each patch:


\operatorname{patch}_i\in\mathbb{R}^{P^2C}


Project to the embedding space:


z_i=W\operatorname{patch}_i+b,\qquad W\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times P^2C}

The resulting patch embeddings act like tokens.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Diffusion Transformers (DiT)
Diffusion Transformers replace the convolutional denoising backbone with a transformer over latent image patches.
Paper: Scalable Diffusion Models with Transformers, Peebles and Xie, 2022.
Key idea:

patchify the noisy latent,
add timestep/class conditioning,
process tokens with DiT blocks,
reshape outputs back to latent noise predictions.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
U-Net vs. DiT








Backbone
Main structure
Strength




U-Net
encoder-decoder with skip connections
strong spatial inductive bias


DiT
transformer over latent patches
scalable global token mixing

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
DiT Architecture


DiT applies transformer blocks to noisy latent patches and uses timestep/class conditioning inside the block.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Latent Diffusion Models
Instead of running diffusion in pixel space, diffuse in a compressed latent space.

z=E(x)

Forward noising:

z_t=\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t}z+\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_t}\epsilon

A U-Net or DiT predicts the noise in latent space, then a decoder reconstructs:

\hat{x}=D(z_0)


Latent diffusion lowers memory cost and makes high-resolution generation more practical.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
What to Remember

Multi-head attention lets different heads learn different relations.
Sampling controls such as temperature and top-K affect generation behavior.
Causal masking prevents future-token leakage during parallel training.
Positional encodings and RoPE give transformers order information.
Transformer blocks combine attention, FFNs, residuals, and normalization.
ViT and DiT show how transformer tokens can represent image patches.

Asset credits

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Autoregressive Models
Autoregressive models generate structured data one piece at a time, conditioning on what they already generated.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
What Is a Modality?
A modality is a type or form of data.



Modality
Examples




Text
sentences, documents


Image
photographs, medical scans


Audio
speech, music


Video
image sequences over time


Multimodal
image plus text, video plus audio

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Generative Task Formats



Input
Output
Examples




Text
Text
Translation, summarization, question answering


Text
Image
Text-to-image synthesis


Text
Audio
Speech or music generation


Image
Text
Captioning, visual QA


Image
Image
Super-resolution, inpainting


Audio
Text
Speech recognition

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Text vs. Images



Text
Images




Sequential
Spatial


1D token structure
2D pixels, often 3D with channels


Sparse and discrete
Dense and continuous


Variable length
Often resized to fixed size


RNNs, LSTMs, transformers
CNNs, diffusion, vision transformers

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
What Means Autoregressive?
“Auto” means the model uses its own previous outputs.
For a sequence:

p(x_1,\ldots,x_T)
=
\prod_{t=1}^{T}p(x_t\mid x_1,\ldots,x_{t-1})


Generation becomes repeated conditional prediction.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Next-Token Prediction
Example:

p(\text{blue}\mid \text{The sky is})


The sky is ? blue

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Autoregressive Generation Loop


function Generate(prompt, model)


sequence = prompt


while not finished


distribution = model(sequence)


next = sample(distribution)


append(sequence, next)


return sequence

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Types of Autoregressive Models



Model
Core mechanism




RNN
Hidden state updated step by step


LSTM
RNN with gates and cell state for long dependencies


GRU
Simpler gated recurrent unit


Transformer decoder
Self-attention over previous tokens


PixelCNN
Masked convolution over previous pixels

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Recurrent Neural Network
An RNN maps:

f_\theta:(x_t,h_{t-1})\mapsto(y_t,h_t)

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Stacked Recurrent Networks
Stacking adds depth at each time step.




Depth helps learn more abstract sequence representations.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
LSTM
LSTMs add gates and a cell state.



Component
Role




Input gate i_t
Controls new information


Forget gate f_t
Controls what to erase


Candidate g_t
Proposed new content


Output gate o_t
Controls exposed hidden state


Cell state c_t
Long-term memory path

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
LSTM Updates

i_t=\sigma(W_{ii}x_t+b_{ii}+W_{hi}h_{t-1}+b_{hi})


f_t=\sigma(W_{if}x_t+b_{if}+W_{hf}h_{t-1}+b_{hf})


g_t=\tanh(W_{ig}x_t+b_{ig}+W_{hg}h_{t-1}+b_{hg})


c_t=f_t\odot c_{t-1}+i_t\odot g_t,\qquad
h_t=o_t\odot\tanh(c_t)

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
GRU
GRU is a simpler gated recurrent unit.







Gate
Purpose




Update gate
Controls how much previous state is kept


Reset gate
Controls how much previous state is used in candidate update




GRUs often train faster than LSTMs while keeping much of the benefit of gated memory.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
PixelCNN
PixelCNN generates images pixel by pixel in raster order.



Masked filters prevent the model from looking at future pixels.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Pixel Mask Intuition



seen
seen
seen


seen
current
future


future
future
future




Autoregressive image generation imposes an ordering on pixels, just like text imposes an ordering on tokens.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
What to Remember

Autoregressive models factor a joint distribution into sequential conditionals.
Generation repeats prediction and sampling.
RNNs summarize history with hidden states.
LSTMs and GRUs improve recurrent memory with gates.
PixelCNN applies autoregression to images using masks.
Transformers will modernize this idea with self-attention.

Asset credits

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
PPO and GRPO
Policy-gradient methods are powerful, but naive policy updates can be unstable.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Where We Are
From policy gradients, the basic update is:

\theta \leftarrow \theta + \alpha \nabla_\theta J(\theta)

The problem:

A gradient step can make the new policy very different from the old one.
A once-good policy can collapse after one overly aggressive update.
We want improvement, but not destructive policy movement.


PPO is built around a simple control knob: keep the new policy close to the policy that collected the data.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Trust Region Intuition
Trust Region Policy Optimization (TRPO) directly constrains policy change:

\max_\theta \; \mathbb{E}_t
\left[
\frac{\pi_\theta(a_t\mid s_t)}
{\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(a_t\mid s_t)}
A_t
\right]
\quad
\text{s.t.}
\quad
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}\,\|\,\pi_\theta)\leq\delta



TRPO

Hard trust-region constraint
More complex optimization
Requires second-order information


PPO

Soft constraint through clipping
Easier first-order optimization
Widely used in practice

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Probability Ratio
PPO compares the new policy to the old policy with:

r_t(\theta)
=
\frac{\pi_\theta(a_t\mid s_t)}
{\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(a_t\mid s_t)}

Interpretation:







Ratio
Meaning




r_t(\theta)=1
New policy gives the sampled action the same probability


r_t(\theta)>1
New policy makes the sampled action more likely


r_t(\theta)<1
New policy makes the sampled action less likely

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
PPO Clipped Objective
PPO maximizes:

L^{\text{PPO}}(\theta)
=
\mathbb{E}_t
\left[
\min\left(
r_t(\theta)A_t,\;
\operatorname{clip}(r_t(\theta),1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)A_t
\right)
\right]


If the policy update tries to move too far, clipping removes the extra incentive.

\epsilon is usually small, often around 0.1 to 0.2.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Why the Min Matters


Positive advantage
If A_t>0, PPO wants to increase the probability of a_t.
Clipping prevents increasing it too much.

Negative advantage
If A_t<0, PPO wants to decrease the probability of a_t.
Clipping prevents decreasing it too much.


The objective is conservative on purpose: accept useful improvement, reject excessive movement.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
PPO Training Loop


theta, phi = initial policy and value parameters


for iteration = 1, 2, …:


D = collectTrajectories(pi_theta)


R_hat, A = estimateReturnsAndAdvantages(D, V_phi)


theta_old = theta


for epoch in 1 … K:


for batch in minibatches(D):


ratio = pi_theta(a|s) / pi_theta_old(a|s)


actorLoss = -mean(min(ratio  A, clip(ratio)  A))


criticLoss = mean((R_hat - V_phi(s))2)


theta, phi = optimizerStep(actorLoss, criticLoss)

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Why PPO Works Well

Stable enough for long training runs.
Simple enough to implement with standard gradient descent.
Reuses collected trajectories for several epochs.
Works with large neural policies.

Common use cases:

Robotics and continuous control
Game playing
RLHF-style language-model training


PPO became popular because it is a practical compromise: not the most theoretically exact, but robust and implementable.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
From PPO to GRPO
PPO usually uses both:

A policy model, the actor.
A value model, the critic.

For large language models, the critic can be expensive:

It adds memory cost.
It adds training complexity.
It can be hard to fit accurately for long reasoning traces.


Can we estimate advantages without training a separate value model?

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
GRPO: Main Idea
Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) samples several responses for the same prompt.
For one prompt q_i:

\{o_{i,1}, o_{i,2}, \dots, o_{i,G}\}
\sim
\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid q_i)

Then compute rewards:

r_{i,j}=r(q_i,o_{i,j})


Instead of asking “how good is this response absolutely?”, GRPO asks “how good is this response compared with the other responses for the same prompt?”

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI

CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
GRPO Training Loop


theta = initial policy parameters


for iteration = 1, 2, …:


prompts = samplePromptBatch()


for each prompt q_i in prompts:


responses = sampleGroup(pi_theta, q_i, G)


rewards = scoreResponses(q_i, responses)


advantages = (rewards - mean(rewards)) / std(rewards)


theta_old = theta


ratio = pi_theta(o|q) / pi_theta_old(o|q)


objective = ppoStyleClippedObjective(ratio, advantages)


theta = optimizerStep(objective)

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
PPO vs. GRPO








Feature
PPO

Assumes access to:

Common Model-Free Methods








Family
Method
Main idea

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Monte Carlo Estimation
Monte Carlo waits until an episode ends, then updates from the full return.

G_t=r_{t+1}+\gamma r_{t+2}+\cdots+\gamma^{T-t-1}r_T


V(s_t)\leftarrow V(s_t)+\alpha\left[G_t-V(s_t)\right]



Strength
Unbiased return estimate under the policy.

Weakness
High variance; must wait for episode end.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text: Monte Carlo vs. TD Timing

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Temporal-Difference Learning
TD learning updates before the episode ends.
It combines:

Learning from raw experience.
Bootstrapping from current value estimates.


“Temporal difference” means the update is driven by the difference between a current estimate and a one-step target.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
TD(0) Target
From the Bellman expectation equation:

V^\pi(s)=\mathbb{E}_\pi[r_{t+1}+\gamma V^\pi(s_{t+1})\mid s_t=s]

Use the sampled target:

r_{t+1}+\gamma V(s_{t+1})

TD(0) update:

V(s_t)\leftarrow V(s_t)+\alpha\left[r_{t+1}+\gamma V(s_{t+1})-V(s_t)\right]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
TD(0) as Algorithm


observe transition (s, r, sNext)


target = r + gamma * V(sNext)


error = target - V(s)


V(s) = V(s) + alpha * error

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
TD(0) Example
Trajectory:

s_1 \xrightarrow{a_1,\;r=1} s_2 \xrightarrow{a_2,\;r=0} s_3

Assume:

\gamma=1,\quad \alpha=0.5,\quad V(s_1)=0,\quad V(s_2)=0.5



V(s_1)\leftarrow 0+0.5[1+0.5-0]=0.75

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
On-Policy vs. Off-Policy



Type
Learns value of
Example




On-policy
The policy being followed
SARSA


Off-policy
A target policy different from behavior
Q-learning




On-policy learns what you do; off-policy learns what you should do.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
SARSA
SARSA uses the tuple:

S \rightarrow A \rightarrow R \rightarrow S' \rightarrow A'

Update:

Q(s_t,a_t)\leftarrow Q(s_t,a_t)+
\alpha\left[
r_{t+1}+\gamma Q(s_{t+1},a_{t+1})-Q(s_t,a_t)
\right]


The next action a_{t+1} is the action actually selected by the behavior policy.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Q-Learning
Q-learning bootstraps toward the best possible next action.

Q(s_t,a_t)\leftarrow Q(s_t,a_t)+
\alpha\left[
r_{t+1}+
\gamma\max_{a'}Q(s_{t+1},a')-
Q(s_t,a_t)
\right]


Q-learning is off-policy because the target is greedy even if the behavior was exploratory.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
SARSA vs. Q-Learning



Method
Target




SARSA
r+\gamma Q(s',a') for the action actually taken


Q-learning
r+\gamma\max_{a'}Q(s',a')

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
TD(n)
TD(n) uses n real rewards before bootstrapping:

G_t^{(n)}
=
r_{t+1}+\gamma r_{t+2}
\cdots+
\gamma^{n-1}r_{t+n}
\gamma^nV(s_{t+n})

Update:

V(s_t)\leftarrow V(s_t)+\alpha\left[G_t^{(n)}-V(s_t)\right]


Larger n usually means lower bias and higher variance.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
TD(lambda)
TD(\lambda) blends all n-step returns:

G_t^{(\lambda)}
=
(1-\lambda)\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\lambda^{n-1}G_t^{(n)}




\lambda
Behavior




0
One-step TD


1
Monte Carlo-like


Between
Smooth bias-variance tradeoff

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Eligibility Traces
Eligibility traces implement TD(\lambda) online.
TD error:

\delta_t=r_{t+1}+\gamma V(s_{t+1})-V(s_t)

Trace update:

e_t(s)=
\begin{cases}
\gamma\lambda e_{t-1}(s)+1,&s=s_t\\
\gamma\lambda e_{t-1}(s),&\text{otherwise}
\end{cases}

Value update:

V(s)\leftarrow V(s)+\alpha\delta_t e_t(s)

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
What to Remember

Monte Carlo learns from full episode returns.
TD learns online by bootstrapping.
SARSA is on-policy.
Q-learning is off-policy.
TD(n) and TD(\lambda) trade bias and variance through multi-step returns.
Eligibility traces assign credit to recently visited states.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Markov Decision Processes
An MDP is a 5-tuple:

(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},\mathcal{P},\mathcal{R},\gamma)




Part
Meaning




\mathcal{S}
States


\mathcal{A}
Actions


\mathcal{P}(s'\mid s,a)
Transition probabilities


\mathcal{R}(s,a)
Reward function


\gamma
Discount factor




Markov property: the next state depends on the current state and action, not the full past.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text: MDP as a Gridworld

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Policies and Values
Policy:

\pi(a \mid s)=P(A_t=a \mid S_t=s)

State value:

V^\pi(s)=
\mathbb{E}_\pi\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^tR_{t+1}\mid S_0=s\right]

Action value:

Q^\pi(s,a)=
\mathbb{E}_\pi\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^tR_{t+1}\mid S_0=s,A_0=a\right]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Finding an Optimal Policy
Goal:

\pi^*=\arg\max_\pi V^\pi(s)

Classical model-based algorithms:

Value iteration.
Policy iteration.


Both rely on Bellman equations: value today equals immediate reward plus discounted future value.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Bellman Equation
For a fixed policy:

V^\pi(s)=
\sum_a \pi(a \mid s)
\sum_{s'}P(s'\mid s,a)
\left[R(s,a)+\gamma V^\pi(s')\right]

For action values:

Q^\pi(s,a)=
\sum_{s'}P(s'\mid s,a)
\left[R(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{a'}\pi(a'\mid s')Q^\pi(s',a')\right]

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Deterministic Optimal Policies
In finite MDPs, if an optimal policy exists, there exists a deterministic optimal policy.
Implications:

We can search over policies that choose one action per state.
Randomization is not required to achieve optimal value.
This simplifies value and policy iteration.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Value Iteration


function ValueIteration(MDP, gamma)


V(s) = 0 for all states


repeat until V converges


for each state s


V(s) = maxa Σs’ P(s’|s,a)[R(s,a) + gammaV(s’)]


return greedy policy from V

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Policy Iteration


function PolicyIteration(MDP, gamma)


pi = arbitrary policy


repeat


Vπ = PolicyEvaluation(pi)


piNew(s) = argmaxa Σs’ P(s’|s,a)[R(s,a) + gammaVπ(s’)]


if piNew == pi return pi


pi = piNew

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Value vs. Policy Iteration








Method
Main update
Tradeoff




Value iteration
Repeated Bellman optimality backups
Cheap iterations, many iterations


Policy iteration
Evaluate policy, then improve policy
Fewer iterations, costlier iterations



Both converge to an optimal policy in finite discounted MDPs.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Example MDP



Discount factor: \gamma=0.9.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Value Iteration: Iteration 3
Using V_2(s_1)=10, V_2(s_2)=8, V_2(s_3)=0:

V_3(s_1)=\max\{5+0.9(8),\;10+0.9(0)\}=12.2


V_3(s_2)=\max\{-1+0.9(10),\;2+0.9(0)\}=8


V_3(s_3)=0


Repeat until the values stabilize.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Policy Iteration Example
Initial policy:

\pi(s_1)=a_1,\qquad \pi(s_2)=a_2,\qquad \pi(s_3)=a_1

Policy evaluation:

V^\pi(s_1)=5+0.9V^\pi(s_2)


V^\pi(s_2)=2+0.9V^\pi(s_3),\qquad V^\pi(s_3)=0

So:

V^\pi(s_1)=6.8,\qquad V^\pi(s_2)=2,\qquad V^\pi(s_3)=0

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Policy Improvement
Use the evaluated values:

\pi_{new}(s_1)=\arg\max\{5+0.9(2),\;10+0.9(0)\}=a_2


\pi_{new}(s_2)=\arg\max\{-1+0.9(6.8),\;2+0.9(0)\}=a_1


After evaluation, improvement makes the policy greedy with respect to the current value function.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
What to Remember

RL learns policies from interaction and reward.
MDPs formalize states, actions, transitions, rewards, and discounting.
Bellman equations express values recursively.
Value iteration updates values directly.
Policy iteration alternates evaluation and improvement.

Deep Learning

Why Deep Learning?
Deep learning matters because it:

Learns features from raw data.
Scales with large datasets and compute.
Works especially well on images, text, audio, and other unstructured data.
Powers systems in vision, speech, language, medical diagnosis, autonomous driving, and generative AI.

predictions = forward(network, inputs)

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Forward Pass
The forward pass computes predictions.
For a single neuron:

z=w_1I_1+w_2I_2+b


O=\text{ReLU}(z)=\max(0,z)

For a layered network:

Each layer computes weighted sums.
Each hidden layer applies nonlinear activations.
The final layer produces the prediction.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Loss Calculation
Loss measures prediction error.


Regression

L=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}(y_i-\hat{y}_i)^2


Classification

L=-\sum_{i=1}^{N} y_i\log(\hat{y}_i)



If \hat{y}=0.8 and y=1, cross-entropy is -\log(0.8)\approx 0.22.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Gradients for One Neuron
Let:

z=w_1I_1+w_2I_2+b,\quad O=\text{ReLU}(z),\quad L=\frac{1}{2}(O-y)^2



\frac{\partial L}{\partial O}=O-y




\frac{\partial O}{\partial z}=\text{ReLU}'(z)=
\begin{cases}
1, & z>0\\
0, & z\leq 0
\end{cases}




\frac{\partial L}{\partial w_1}=(O-y)\text{ReLU}'(z)I_1

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Weight Update
Gradient descent updates each parameter in the direction that reduces loss:

w_i := w_i-\eta\frac{\partial L}{\partial w_i}

For the single neuron:

w_1 := w_1-\eta(O-y)\text{ReLU}'(z)I_1


b := b-\eta(O-y)\text{ReLU}'(z)


If \eta is too large, training can diverge. If it is too small, training is slow.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
What to Remember

Deep networks learn layered representations.
A neuron computes a weighted sum, bias, and nonlinear activation.
Training alternates forward pass, loss, backpropagation, and optimization.
Backpropagation uses the chain rule to compute gradients.
Learning rate controls update size.

title:

(Intro to) AI
text:
Learning Decision Trees
We want a tree that is:

Accurate on training examples.
Small enough to generalize.
Cheap enough to build.
Fast enough to evaluate.


But the space of possible trees is enormous.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Space of Trees
With n Boolean attributes, the number of possible decision trees is more than:

2^{2^n}

So we do not search exhaustively.

Decision-tree learning usually uses a greedy construction method: choose one split, recurse, and do not backtrack.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI

CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Purity and Entropy
We want splits that create pure groups.


Low entropy
Most examples have the same label.
Prediction is easier.

High entropy
Labels are mixed.
Prediction is uncertain.


Information gain measures how much a split reduces entropy.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Entropy
Entropy of a set S:

H(S)=-\sum_{i=1}^{m} p_i\log_2 p_i

where p_i is the fraction of examples with class label i.
Examples:

Fair coin: 1 bit.
Two-headed coin: 0 bits.
99 percent heads coin: about 0.0808 bits.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Information Gain
For an attribute A:

IG(S,A)=H(S)-\sum_{v \in \text{Values}(A)}\frac{|S_v|}{|S|}H(S_v)

where S_v is the subset with A=v.




Choose the split that most reduces expected entropy.

(Intro to) AI
text:
Overfitting and Pruning
Decision trees can overfit by creating branches that explain noise.
Pruning simplifies a tree after it is built.


Benefits

Smaller trees.
Easier interpretation.
Better generalization.


\chi^2 pruning
Remove a split if its reduction in impurity is not statistically significant.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Why Not Prune Early?
If a split has low immediate information gain, why not avoid it?

Because some useful patterns require combinations of attributes.


A first split might look weak, but it can enable a strong second split.


Post-pruning lets the tree discover interactions before simplifying.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
What to Remember

Decision trees classify by following attribute tests from root to leaf.
Greedy tree induction avoids exhaustive search.
Entropy measures label uncertainty.
Information gain measures entropy reduction from a split.
Pruning combats overfitting and can improve generalization.

title:

text:
k-Nearest Neighbors
k-NN is an instance-based supervised learning algorithm.

To classify a new point, find the k closest training examples and let them vote.

It is simple, useful, and a good first example of how “learning” can be stored in the training data itself.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
k-NN Algorithm


function KNNPredict(query, trainingData, k)


distances = []


for each (x, label) in trainingData


append(distances, (distance(query, x), label))


neighbors = kSmallest(distances, k)


return majorityVote(neighbors)

Probabilistic Inference
Probabilistic inference computes unknown probabilities from known distributions and evidence.

(Intro to) AI
text:
What Is Inference?

Probabilistic inference answers queries such as P(\text{Query} \mid \text{Evidence}).

Examples:

Given an umbrella observation, infer the probability of rain.
Given robot sensor readings, infer the robot’s location.
Given user behavior, infer a likely preference.


The distribution is the model; inference is how we ask questions of the model.

Toy Boolean variables:

Query 1: P(C \lor T)
It is easier to use the complement:

P(C \lor T)=1-P(\neg C,\neg T)


From the full joint table:

P(\neg C,\neg T)=P(\neg C,\neg T,H)+P(\neg C,\neg T,\neg H)




P(\neg C,\neg T)=0.144+0.576=0.72

Marginalization
To compute a marginal, sum out variables that are not in the query.

P(C)=\sum_T\sum_H P(C,T,H)


For the cavity row:

P(C)=0.108+0.012+0.072+0.008=0.2



“Summing out” reduces a distribution over many variables to a distribution over fewer variables.

CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI

Query 2: P(C \mid T)
Keep T=\text{true} and sum over both values of H.



Quantity
Matching joint mass




Numerator P(C,T)
0.108+0.012=0.12

0.016+0.064=0.08

For query outcomes ordered as (C,\neg C), first collect joint masses:

w=(0.12,0.08).


Normalize with:

\alpha=\frac{1}{0.12+0.08}=5




\bigl(P(C\mid T),P(\neg C\mid T)\bigr)=(0.6,0.4).



Normalization divides nonnegative weights by their positive sum. Here that sum is the evidence probability P(T).

The relative ratio stays the same; only the total mass is rescaled.

Why Normalization Helps


Validity

Probabilities must sum to 1.
Normalization rescales values without changing their relative order.


Computation

Often the denominator is expensive.
We compute proportional values first.
Then normalize at the end.

Softmax as Normalization
Softmax turns logits into probabilities:

\text{softmax}(z_i)=\frac{e^{z_i}}{\sum_j e^{z_j}}



Used in classification
The output layer maps raw scores to class probabilities.

Used in transformers
Attention scores become attention weights; output logits become token probabilities.

2^n

entries.

10

The table is exact, but exactness becomes useless if we cannot store or query it.

The Need for Structure
Full joint inference requires summing many entries.
Structured representations reduce the work by exploiting conditional independence.





Cavity CToothache TProbe catches H


P(C,T,H)=P(C)P(T\mid C)P(H\mid C).

Bayesian networks can store the distribution compactly. Exact inference can still be expensive, depending on the graph.

(Intro to) AI
text:
What to Remember

Full joint distributions answer any probability query in principle.
Marginalization sums out variables.
Conditioning divides by the evidence probability.
Normalization rescales relative values into probabilities.
Full joint tables grow exponentially, so we need structured models.

Planning Algorithms
Last time: how to describe a planning problem. Today: how to solve one.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
From Representation to Search
A planning problem gives us:



Part
Example




Initial state
\text{on}(A,\text{Table}) \land \text{on}(C,A)


Actions
\text{move}(b,\text{from},\text{to})


Goal
\text{on}(A,B) \land \text{on}(B,C)



The algorithm must decide which action sequence reaches the goal.

Planning algorithms differ mainly in what they search over: states, goals, graphs, formulas, or task decompositions.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Main Families








Family
Search object
Typical idea




Progression
Current states
Start at the initial state and apply actions


Regression
Goal descriptions
Start at the goal and ask what must be true before


Planning graph
Alternating fact/action layers
Grow a relaxed reachability structure


SAT planning
Boolean variables over time
Ask if a length-T plan exists


HTN planning
Tasks and methods
Decompose abstract tasks into primitive actions

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
State-Space Planning


Progression

Forward search.
Nodes are concrete states.
Actions generate successor states.
Goal test checks the current state.


Regression

Backward search.
Nodes are goal descriptions.
Actions explain how goals could be achieved.
Stop when the initial state satisfies the regressed goals.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Progression Search


function ProgressionSearch(initial, goal, actions)


frontier = [initial]


while frontier is not empty


state = pop(frontier)


if satisfies(state, goal) return plan(state)


for each action applicable in state


push(frontier, result(state, action))


return failure



Progression is natural, but it may spend time on actions unrelated to the goal.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Progression Example





Blocks world planning example



Goal:

\text{on}(A,B) \land \text{on}(B,C)

Plan:

\text{move}(C,B,\text{Table})
\text{move}(B,A,C)
\text{move}(A,\text{Table},B)

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Progression as a Path




Forward search asks: what can I do now?

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Regression Search


function RegressionSearch(initial, goal, actions)


frontier = [goal]


while frontier is not empty


subgoal = pop(frontier)


if satisfies(initial, subgoal) return reversedPlan(subgoal)


for each action that achieves part of subgoal


push(frontier, regress(subgoal, action))


return failure



Regression is often helpful when the goal is small and most actions are irrelevant.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Regression Example
Goal:

\text{on}(A,B) \land \text{on}(B,C)


\text{move}(A,\text{Table},B) can achieve \text{on}(A,B), but it requires \text{clear}(B).


\text{move}(B,\text{Table},C) can achieve \text{on}(B,C), and it must happen before A moves onto B.


To make that possible, first clear C by moving it away.


Regression explains the plan from the goal backward, then executes it forward.

Boolean Satisfiability
SAT asks whether a Boolean formula has a satisfying assignment.

(A \lor B) \land (\neg A \lor C) \land (\neg B \lor \neg C)



Why it matters

SAT is NP-complete.
Modern SAT solvers are very strong in practice.


Planning connection

Turn a bounded planning problem into a formula.
A satisfying assignment encodes a plan.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
SAT-Based Planning


function SATPlan(initial, goal, actions)


for T = 0, 1, 2, …


formula = encodePlanningProblem(initial, goal, actions, T)


assignment = SATsolver(formula)


if assignment exists


return extractActions(assignment)

CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
SAT Encoding Ingredients
For a horizon T, create variables such as:

\text{on}(A,B,t), \qquad \text{move}(A,B,C,t)

Then add constraints:







Constraint type
Meaning




Initial state
Facts true at t=0


Goal
Goal facts true at t=T


Preconditions
If an action occurs, its preconditions held


Effects
Actions make add/delete effects true


Frame/action constraints
Facts persist unless changed; actions do not conflict

Heuristics estimate distance to the goal.


Common idea
Relax the problem, solve or approximate the relaxed version, and use that as a guide.

Examples

A* planning.
FF: Fast Forward heuristic.
Planning graph heuristics.



Good heuristics keep the planner from expanding many irrelevant states.

HTN planning decomposes tasks instead of searching directly over primitive actions.

Role

Ordering and dependency structure among tasks




HTN planning uses domain knowledge to guide the decomposition, which can be powerful when good methods are available.

CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI

What to Remember

Progression searches forward from the initial state.
Regression searches backward from the goal.
Planning graphs and heuristics expose useful reachability information.
SAT planning asks whether a plan of length T exists.
HTN planning solves abstract tasks by decomposition.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Planning
Planning asks an agent to reason before acting: which sequence of actions will transform the current world into a goal world?

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
What Is Planning?

Planning is reasoning about a sequence of actions that achieves a goal.



We represent

The initial state.
Action templates.
Preconditions.
Effects.
The goal.


We search for

A sequence of ground actions.
Each action applicable when used.
A final state satisfying the goal.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
section: Why Planning Gets Its Own Representation
text:
Why Planning Gets Its Own Representation
Planning uses a restricted logic-like language so search can exploit structure.



Component
Planning view




State
A conjunction of function-free predicate literals


Action
Preconditions plus effects


Goal
A conjunction of facts that must hold


Quantifiers
Avoided in the action/state language




The restriction is a feature: it makes action applicability and goal checking mechanical.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
A Tiny Robot Example


State and Goal

\text{At}(\text{Robot},A) \land \text{Connected}(A,B)


\text{Goal}: \text{At}(\text{Robot},B)


Action

\text{Move}(A,B)

Precondition:

\text{At}(\text{Robot},A) \land \text{Connected}(A,B)

Effect:

\neg \text{At}(\text{Robot},A) \land \text{At}(\text{Robot},B)

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Blocks World


Blocks world is a small planning domain:

Labeled blocks sit on a table.
Blocks can be stacked.
A block can move only if nothing is on top of it.
The goal describes a desired arrangement.


Small domain, large search space. That is exactly why it is useful for planning.





Blocks world start and goal illustration

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Blocks World Predicates



Symbol
Meaning




\text{Table}
The table constant


\text{block}(A)
A is a block


\text{on}(A,B)
A is on B


\text{on}(A,\text{Table})
A is on the table


\text{clear}(A)
Nothing is stacked on A




Planning will use these facts directly; facts not listed as true are treated as false.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Initial State


The initial state is a set of true facts:

\text{block}(A) \land \text{block}(B) \land \text{block}(C)


\text{on}(B,\text{Table}) \land \text{on}(C,A) \land \text{on}(A,\text{Table})





Blocks world initial state




Closed world assumption: if \text{on}(B,A) is not stated, the planner treats it as false.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Goal State
The goal is usually partial.

\text{on}(A,B) \land \text{on}(B,C)



Specified

A must be on B.
B must be on C.


Not specified

Where C is.
Which other clear facts hold.
Other irrelevant facts.



Many complete final states can satisfy one partial goal.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
First Try: A Move Template
The natural action template is:


move(b, from, to)


pre: block(b) and on(b, from)


and no block is on b


and no block is on to


effect: on(b, to) and not on(b, from)



But “no block is on …” sounds like a quantifier. The planning language is supposed to avoid quantifiers.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Reifying “Nothing On Top”
Instead of writing:

\neg \exists x\; \text{on}(x,b)

we introduce a predicate:

\text{clear}(b)



Before
“No object is on b.”
This is quantified.

After
“b is clear.”
This is a simple fact.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Move Onto Another Object


move(b, from, to)


pre: block(b)


and on(b, from)


and clear(b)


and clear(to)


effect: on(b, to)


and not on(b, from)


and not clear(to)


and clear(from)

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Move Onto the Table
The table is a special destination: it can hold multiple blocks.


moveToTable(b, from)


pre: block(b)


and on(b, from)


and clear(b)


effect: on(b, Table)


and not on(b, from)


and clear(from)



Separating table moves keeps the action schema faithful to the domain.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
From Templates to Ground Actions
Action templates contain variables. A plan uses ground actions.


Template

\text{moveToTable}(b,\text{from})

Ground action

\text{moveToTable}(C,A)


Grounded preconditions

\text{block}(C) \land \text{on}(C,A) \land \text{clear}(C)

Grounded effects

\text{on}(C,\text{Table}) \land \neg \text{on}(C,A) \land \text{clear}(A)

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Finding a Plan
Goal:

\text{on}(A,B) \land \text{on}(B,C)



\text{moveToTable}(C,A): move C off A.




\text{move}(B,\text{Table},C): move B onto C.




\text{move}(A,\text{Table},B): move A onto B.



Each action must be applicable when it is executed; the sequence matters.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Problem Size
Suppose there are 6 objects: blocks plus table.








Template
Parameters
Ground instances




\text{move}(\text{block}, \text{from}, \text{to})
3
6^3 = 216


\text{moveToTable}(\text{block}, \text{from})
2
6^2 = 36


Total

252




Many of these ground actions may be illegal in a state, but the planner still has to reason about a large candidate space.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
Complexity of Planning
Planning is difficult in general.


Theoretical results

General planning is PSPACE-complete.
Optimal planning is often NP-hard.


Practical pressure

State spaces grow exponentially.
Preconditions constrain search.
Actions interact through their effects.



The next question is how to search this space intelligently.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
text:
What to Remember

Planning searches over action sequences, not single actions.
States, goals, preconditions, and effects are represented as predicate literals.
Action templates become ground actions by replacing variables with objects.
The closed world assumption makes missing facts false.
Even simple domains create many possible ground actions.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
section: Can the Robot Conclude It May Move?
text:
Can the Robot Conclude It May Move?


Let B = battery ready, C = corridor clear, and M = movement permitted.
The robot knows:

B, \qquad (B \land C) \rightarrow M


Must M be true? Must M be false? Or is it still undetermined?





Take a quick vote without revealing the answer yet. The intended answer is undetermined. We know B, but lack information about C and M. Do not read the implication as a biconditional. M is a proposition about permission, not an instruction that is executed automatically. The example will return at the end.
50-minute teaching plan, including discussion and answer reveals:

Slides 1-8: facts, models, entailment, and counterexamples (11 minutes).
Slides 9-16: query exercise, formula classification, SAT, and model checking (14 minutes).
Slides 17-24: inference rules, CNF practice, and resolution (14 minutes).
Slides 25-31: refutation, common mistakes, and the robot exit exercise (11 minutes).

Keep the three main activities on slides 9, 21, and 29 interactive. Students should justify an answer with a model, equivalence, or proof step, not just name a result. This lecture builds on Lecture 16 and prepares the propositional foundations needed for Lecture 18 and Homework 3; the examples are not the homework solutions.

(Intro to) AI
text:
Facts, Rules, and a Query
A knowledge base (KB) is a collection of sentences assumed true.



Role
Robot example




Fact
B


Rule
(B \land C) \rightarrow M


Query
Does M follow from the KB?



We read all KB sentences together as a conjunction:

\text{KB} = B \land \bigl((B \land C) \rightarrow M\bigr)


Inference asks what follows from the sentences, not what seems plausible.


Clarify that rules and facts are both formulas. Writing KB as a set or as their conjunction is a representational choice. The assumed facts could be wrong about the physical world; inference guarantees a consequence of the encoded premises, not the correctness of the sensors.
[Sources]

AIMA Chapter 7, knowledge-based agents. Original robot encoding.

(Intro to) AI

T and F abbreviate true and false. Textbooks also call a full assignment a model and then say it satisfies or fails to satisfy a formula. Here, compatible world always means satisfying assignment. Ask students to identify the excluded row before explaining it.

Entailment Means Every Compatible World

\text{KB} \models \alpha

The query \alpha is true in every model of the KB.

Alpha names the query formula; it need not be a single atom. Explain the set inclusion visually. The reverse inclusion is not required: the query may hold in worlds that violate the KB.

\text{KB} \models Q. No row makes the KB true and the query false.


Have students find the rows where the complete KB is true, not merely where one rule is true. There is exactly one such row. This is a semantic verification of modus ponens, which we will name later.

title:

(Intro to) AI
text:
One Counterexample Is Enough
Now reverse the proposed reasoning:

\text{KB} = Q \land (P \rightarrow Q), \qquad \alpha = P




Assignment
KB true?
Query P true?




P=\text{true},\ Q=\text{true}
Yes

Yes

\text{KB} \not\models P. The second row is a countermodel: a model of the KB that falsifies the query.


This is the fallacy of affirming the consequent. One supporting example never proves entailment, but one countermodel disproves it. The two listed assignments exhaust the KB’s models over P and Q.
[Sources]

Original countermodel example. AIMA Chapter 7, entailment.

title:
CS 463G & CS 663
(Intro to) AI
section: Not Entailed Does Not Mean False
text:
Not Entailed Does Not Mean False
Return to \text{KB}=B\land((B\land C)\rightarrow M).
Both of these assignments satisfy it:



B
C
M
Compatible with KB?




T
F

\text{KB} \not\models M
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\text{KB} \not\models \neg M



The truth of M is undetermined by the KB. Missing information is not automatically false.


These are two witnesses, not an exhaustive list: B=true, C=true, M=true is also a model. The three cases supported, refuted, and undetermined describe our information; they do not introduce a third truth value into classical propositional logic. A closed-world convention would be an additional assumption, not the default here.
