title: Linear Regression and Generalization
text:
Questions to Explore

Why does using fewer than ten features omit part of the true signal?
Why can training error keep falling while test error rises?
Change the noise level and rerun the experiment. Which part of the theoretical expression changes?
Why might a small number of trials give an unstable average near interpolation?



Answers and discussion


The omitted features carry real signal. The response uses the first ten feature coordinates with nonzero coefficients. A fit with p < 10 cannot represent the contribution from coordinates p through 9. Because the features are independent Gaussian variables, that omitted contribution has variance sum(beta_star[p:] ** 2) and cannot be recovered from the included features alone.
Fitting noise is not generalization. Adding features cannot worsen the best achievable training least-squares fit, and enough features can interpolate the noisy training responses. Near the interpolation threshold, poorly determined directions can amplify noise and make predictions unstable on independent test examples. Thus training error can fall while test error rises; the full test-error curve need not be monotone on either side of the threshold.
The noise-dependent terms change with sigma squared. The omitted-signal term and coefficient norm stay fixed. The irreducible noise variance and the noise-amplification terms all depend on sigma ** 2. Doubling sigma quadruples those contributions; for example, the irreducible error changes from 0.04 to 0.16. It does not quadruple any separate signal-bias contribution.
Rare unstable fits can dominate a small average. Near interpolation, a random design can have very small singular values. Taking their reciprocals in the pseudoinverse amplifies noise and can produce exceptionally large test errors. A small set of trials may include or miss such cases, making its mean and min-to-max band unstable. More trials help away from the excluded singular cases, but do not turn a divergent expected error into a finite one.


Takeaway: training fit, model size, and generalization are not interchangeable. The estimator and the data-generating assumptions matter.

title: Backpropagation by Hand
text:
Inputs, Parameters, and Learning Rate
The input has shape (1, 2) and the target has shape (1, 1): one example with two features and one response. requires_grad=True tells PyTorch to track operations on the learnable weights and biases.
The hidden weight matrix has shape (2, 1); the output weight has shape (1, 1). Biases are added by broadcasting. The seed reproduces initialization, and the learning rate sets the size of the eventual update.

import torch

# Set random seed for reproducibility
torch.manual_seed(42)

# Define input (2 features) and target output (scalar)
X = torch.tensor([[0.5, 1.0]], dtype=torch.float32)  # Input shape: (1,2)
y = torch.tensor([[1.0]], dtype=torch.float32)       # Target shape: (1,1)

# Initialize weights and bias
w1 = torch.randn((2, 1), requires_grad=True)  # Weights for input layer (2 → 1 hidden unit)
b1 = torch.zeros(1, requires_grad=True)       # Bias for hidden layer

w2 = torch.randn((1, 1), requires_grad=True)  # Weights for hidden layer → output
b2 = torch.zeros(1, requires_grad=True)       # Bias for output layer

# Learning rate
lr = 0.1

title: Backpropagation by Hand
text:
Hidden Layer
First compute z_1=Xw_1+b_1. The rectified linear unit (ReLU) activation keeps positive values and replaces negative ones with zero: a_1=\max(0,z_1).
For this one-unit network, both intermediate tensors have shape (1, 1).

# Step 1: Forward Pass (Layer 1 - Hidden Layer)
z1 = X @ w1 + b1  # Linear transformation
a1 = torch.relu(z1)  # Activation function (ReLU)

title: Backpropagation by Hand
text:
Output and Loss
The output layer is linear: O=a_1w_2+b_2. The code uses mean squared error (MSE) with no factor of one half. There is one scalar prediction, so L=(O-y)^2 and \partial L/\partial O=2(O-y).
The printed prediction and loss are measured before any parameter update.

# Step 2: Forward Pass (Layer 2 - Output Layer)
z2 = a1 @ w2 + b2  # Linear transformation
output = z2  # Final output

# Step 3: Compute Loss (Mean Squared Error)
loss = torch.mean((output - y) ** 2)

# Print forward pass results
print(f"Output before backpropagation: {output.item():.4f}")
print(f"Loss before backpropagation: {loss.item():.4f}")


Output before backpropagation: 0.0697
Loss before backpropagation: 0.8655

title: Backpropagation by Hand
text:
Ask Autograd for Gradients
loss.backward() traverses the computation graph and accumulates derivatives in each leaf parameter’s .grad field. It does not change parameter values. We retain these gradients to compare against the manual calculation.

# Step 4: Backward Pass (Compute Gradients)
loss.backward()  # Automatically computes gradients using backpropagation

title: Backpropagation by Hand
text:
Compute the Chain Rule Manually
Let \delta_2=2(O-y). The output is linear, so
\frac{\partial L}{\partial w_2}=a_1\delta_2, \qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial b_2}=\delta_2.
The hidden error is \delta_1=\delta_2 w_2\,\mathbb{1}[z_1>0], giving
\frac{\partial L}{\partial w_1}=X^\top\delta_1, \qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial b_1}=\delta_1.
PyTorch uses derivative zero for ReLU at zero. The code’s Boolean mask follows that convention. torch.no_grad() prevents these manual calculations from creating another autograd graph.
The elementwise products below work for this single-example, single-hidden-unit network. Larger batches and layers require appropriate matrix products and sums over examples.

with torch.no_grad():
    # Step 5: Compute Manual Gradients
    dL_dO = 2 * (output - y) / 1  # Derivative of MSE loss w.r.t. output
    dO_dz2 = 1  # Since output = z2, its derivative is 1
    dL_dz2 = dL_dO * dO_dz2  # Chain rule

    # Gradients for w2 and b2 (Output layer)
    dL_dw2 = dL_dz2 * a1  # dL/dw2 = dL/dz2 * da1/dw2
    dL_db2 = dL_dz2 * 1    # dL/db2 = dL/dz2 * db2/db2

    # Gradients for w1 and b1 (Hidden layer)
    dz2_da1 = w2  # Derivative of z2 w.r.t. a1 (weights from hidden to output layer)
    da1_dz1 = (z1 > 0).float()  # ReLU derivative (1 if z1 > 0, else 0)

    dL_dz1 = dL_dz2 * dz2_da1 * da1_dz1  # Chain rule: dL/dz1 = dL/dz2 * dz2/da1 * da1/dz1
    dL_dw1 = dL_dz1 * X.T  # dL/dw1 = dL/dz1 * X
    dL_db1 = dL_dz1 * 1  # dL/db1 = dL/dz1 * db1/db1

title: Backpropagation by Hand
text:
Compare the Four Parameter Gradients
Compare the automatic and manual entries for both weights and both biases. The first-layer weight gradient has two entries because the hidden unit receives two features. The saved combined log is displayed after the final forward pass below.

# Print Gradients
print("\nAutomatic Gradients (PyTorch):")
print(f"dL/dw1: {w1.grad}")
print(f"dL/db1: {b1.grad}")
print(f"dL/dw2: {w2.grad}")
print(f"dL/db2: {b2.grad}")

print("\nManual Gradients (Calculated using Chain Rule):")
print(f"dL/dw1: {dL_dw1}")
print(f"dL/db1: {dL_db1}")
print(f"dL/dw2: {dL_dw2}")
print(f"dL/db2: {dL_db2}")

title: Backpropagation by Hand
text:
Check Numerical Agreement
torch.allclose checks agreement within floating-point tolerances. All four checks should be True. A missing factor of two in the MSE derivative would fail this comparison.
Some manual bias gradients retain a (1, 1) shape while the parameter gradients have shape (1,); this comparison allows broadcasting. Values agree here, but shape checks also matter when extending the network.

# Step 6: Verify Matching
print("\nChecking if manual and automatic gradients match:")
print(torch.allclose(w1.grad, dL_dw1), "for dL/dw1")
print(torch.allclose(b1.grad, dL_db1), "for dL/db1")
print(torch.allclose(w2.grad, dL_dw2), "for dL/dw2")
print(torch.allclose(b2.grad, dL_db2), "for dL/db2")

title: Backpropagation by Hand
text:
Take a Gradient-Descent Step
Each parameter follows \theta\leftarrow\theta-\eta\nabla_\theta L. The update occurs inside no_grad(), since changing the parameters is not part of the next differentiation graph.
The gradients are then zeroed because PyTorch accumulates them by default. Rerunning the comparison after this cell would compare against zeroed gradients; restart from initialization for a fresh full comparison.

# Step 7: Update Weights (Gradient Descent)
with torch.no_grad():
    w1 -= lr * w1.grad
    b1 -= lr * b1.grad
    w2 -= lr * w2.grad
    b2 -= lr * b2.grad

    # Zero out gradients after update
    w1.grad.zero_()
    b1.grad.zero_()
    w2.grad.zero_()
    b2.grad.zero_()

title: Backpropagation by Hand
text:
Recompute the Prediction
Run the forward equations again with the updated parameters and measure a new loss. The saved log contains the earlier gradient values, the four agreement checks, and the prediction and loss after the update.
A smaller loss in this example confirms that the chosen update helped on this example. An excessively large learning rate can increase loss even when the gradient is correct.

# Step 8: Forward Pass Again (After Weight Update)
z1 = X @ w1 + b1
a1 = torch.relu(z1)
z2 = a1 @ w2 + b2
new_output = z2

# Compute new loss
new_loss = torch.mean((new_output - y) ** 2)

# Print updated results
print(f"\nOutput after weight update: {new_output.item():.4f}")
print(f"Loss after weight update: {new_loss.item():.4f}")


Automatic Gradients (PyTorch):
dL/dw1: tensor([[-0.2181],
        [-0.4363]])
dL/db1: tensor([-0.4363])
dL/dw2: tensor([[-0.5529]])
dL/db2: tensor([-1.8607])

Manual Gradients (Calculated using Chain Rule):
dL/dw1: tensor([[-0.2181],
        [-0.4363]])
dL/db1: tensor([[-0.4363]])
dL/dw2: tensor([[-0.5529]])
dL/db2: tensor([[-1.8607]])

Checking if manual and automatic gradients match:
True for dL/dw1
True for dL/db1
True for dL/dw2
True for dL/db2

Output after weight update: 0.3006
Loss after weight update: 0.4891

title: Backpropagation by Hand
text:
Check Your Understanding

Which operations compute gradients, which modify weights, and which clear accumulated gradients?
If the hidden preactivation were negative, which weight gradients would become zero? Could the output bias still learn?
Why does MSE averaged over several outputs require dividing its derivative by the number of averaged elements?



Answers and discussion


Gradient calculation, parameter update, and reset are separate. loss.backward() accumulates automatic gradients in .grad; the explicit chain-rule expressions compute the manual versions. The statements such as w1 -= lr * w1.grad change parameters. Calls such as w1.grad.zero_() clear the stored gradients. torch.no_grad() only disables graph tracking for operations inside its block; it neither clears gradients nor updates parameters by itself.
A negative hidden preactivation blocks this unit’s gradient. ReLU gives a1 = 0 and derivative zero. Both entries of the w1 gradient and the b1 gradient become zero. The w2 gradient is also zero because its input a1 is zero. The output bias still has gradient 2(O-y), so it can learn unless the prediction already matches the target.
Differentiation preserves the averaging factor. For m scalar output elements, MSE is the sum of their squared errors divided by m. The derivative for element i is therefore 2(O_i-y_i)/m. Omitting the division differentiates the sum of squared errors instead, scaling the gradient by m and making the update magnitude depend on how many elements were averaged. Here m is one.


Takeaway: backpropagation computes derivatives; gradient descent uses them. Keeping those two steps separate makes training code easier to debug.

title: Convolutional Neural Network Demo
text:
Imports and Random Seed
The data loader batches examples, torch.nn supplies layers and loss functions, and torch.optim supplies the optimizer. The seed helps reproduce initialization and shuffling, although results can still vary across devices and software versions.

import torch
from torchvision import datasets, transforms
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.optim as optim
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# set random seed for reproducibility
torch.manual_seed(42)

title: Convolutional Neural Network Demo
section: Define Layers and the Forward Pass
text:
Define Layers and the Forward Pass
__init__ creates the learnable layers. forward specifies how an input moves through them. The class stays together as a complete Python definition.
PyTorch uses tensor order (batch, channels, height, width). For a batch of size B, the shape changes are:








Stage
Output shape
Role




Input
B x 1 x 28 x 28
Grayscale images


First convolution + ReLU
B x 32 x 28 x 28
Local feature maps


Second convolution + ReLU
B x 64 x 28 x 28
Combine local features


Max pooling
B x 64 x 14 x 14
Reduce spatial resolution


Flatten
B x 12544
One feature vector per image


Fully connected + ReLU
B x 128
Learned classifier features


Dropout + output layer
B x 10
One score per digit



ReLU means rectified linear unit. Padding preserves spatial size in both convolutions; pooling occurs only after the second. Dropout randomly suppresses hidden activations during training. The final scores are logits, not probabilities.

# Define the CNN model
class CNN(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super(CNN, self).__init__()
        self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(1, 32, kernel_size=3, stride=1, padding=1) # size 28x28x1 -> 28x28x32
        self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(32, 64, kernel_size=3, stride=1, padding=1) # size 28x28x32 -> 28x28x64
        self.pool = nn.MaxPool2d(kernel_size=2, stride=2) # size 28x28x64 -> 14x14x64
        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(64 * 14 * 14, 128)
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(128, 10)
        self.relu = nn.ReLU()
        self.dropout = nn.Dropout(0.5)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.relu(self.conv1(x))
        x = self.pool(self.relu(self.conv2(x)))
        x = x.view(-1, 64 * 14 * 14)
        x = self.relu(self.fc1(x))
        x = self.dropout(x)
        x = self.fc2(x)
        return x

title: Convolutional Neural Network Demo
text:
Load and Normalize Images
MNIST is the Modified National Institute of Standards and Technology digit dataset. Tensor conversion maps pixels to [0, 1]; normalization maps them to [-1, 1]. Both data splits use identical preprocessing.
Unlike the KNN notebook’s single-batch subset, these loaders are iterated over completely. Training batches are shuffled; test batches are not. A smaller final batch is allowed.

# Load MNIST dataset
transform = transforms.Compose([
    transforms.ToTensor(),
    transforms.Normalize((0.5,), (0.5,))
])

train_dataset = datasets.MNIST(root='~/temp_data', train=True, transform=transform, download=True)
test_dataset = datasets.MNIST(root='~/temp_data', train=False, transform=transform, download=True)

train_loader = DataLoader(train_dataset, batch_size=64, shuffle=True)
test_loader = DataLoader(test_dataset, batch_size=64, shuffle=False)

title: Convolutional Neural Network Demo
text:
Model, Loss, and Optimizer
The model and each batch must be on the same device. CrossEntropyLoss consumes raw logits and integer class labels; do not insert a softmax before this loss.
Adam updates the model’s parameters using gradients and running moment estimates. Its learning rate is 0.001. Constructing the optimizer does not train the model.

# Initialize model, loss function, and optimizer
device = torch.device('cuda' if torch.cuda.is_available() else 'cpu')
model = CNN().to(device)
criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
optimizer = optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=0.001)

title: Convolutional Neural Network Demo
text:
Train for One Epoch
One epoch visits the whole training set once. model.train() enables training behavior, including dropout. For each batch:

Move images and labels to the selected device.
Clear old gradients with zero_grad().
Compute logits and cross-entropy loss.
Backpropagate with loss.backward().
Update parameters with optimizer.step().

The printed loss is the mean of batch loss values. Since the last batch can be smaller, it is not an exactly sample-weighted dataset mean.

# Training loop
num_epochs = 1
for epoch in range(num_epochs):
    model.train()
    running_loss = 0.0
    for images, labels in train_loader:
        images, labels = images.to(device), labels.to(device)
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        outputs = model(images)
        loss = criterion(outputs, labels)
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()
        running_loss += loss.item()
    print(f"Epoch {epoch+1}/{num_epochs}, Loss: {running_loss/len(train_loader)}")


Epoch 1/1, Loss: 0.2424318811405442

title: Convolutional Neural Network Demo
text:
Prepare Held-Out Evaluation
model.eval() disables dropout. Counters record the number of correct predictions and total test examples. The lists retain the first three errors for later inspection.
Evaluation mode and gradient tracking are different controls: the next cell also uses no_grad() to avoid building backward graphs.

# Evaluation
model.eval()
correct = 0
total = 0
wrong_images = []
wrong_labels = []
wrong_predictions = []

title: Convolutional Neural Network Demo
text:
Predict Without Updating Weights
For each image, the index of the largest logit is the predicted digit. Correct predictions are counted across the entire test set. Misclassified images and labels are copied back to the CPU for plotting.
No backward call or optimizer step occurs here. The test labels measure performance; they are not used to train on these examples.

with torch.no_grad():
    for images, labels in test_loader:
        images, labels = images.to(device), labels.to(device)
        outputs = model(images)
        _, predicted = torch.max(outputs, 1)
        total += labels.size(0)
        correct += (predicted == labels).sum().item()
        
        if len(wrong_images) < 3:  # Collect wrong predictions
            # Collect wrong predictions
            for i in range(len(labels)):
                if predicted[i] != labels[i]:
                    wrong_images.append(images[i].cpu())
                    wrong_labels.append(labels[i].cpu())
                    wrong_predictions.append(predicted[i].cpu())
                    if len(wrong_images) == 3:  # Stop after collecting 3 wrong images
                        break

title: Convolutional Neural Network Demo
text:
Inspect Misclassifications
The displayed images are the first three errors encountered, not a random or representative sample. Compare the true and predicted digits: an aggregate accuracy cannot reveal the appearance of individual failures.
This plotting code assumes that at least three errors were collected, which holds for the saved run. A more accurate model or a smaller evaluation subset would need a length check.

# Display 3 wrong images
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(6, 2))
for i, ax in enumerate(axes):
    ax.imshow(wrong_images[i].squeeze(), cmap='gray')
    ax.set_title(f"True: {wrong_labels[i].item()}, Pred: {wrong_predictions[i].item()}")
    ax.axis('off')
plt.show()

title: Convolutional Neural Network Demo
text:
Report Test Accuracy
Accuracy divides the total number correct by the number of test images, then expresses the result as a percentage. This is held-out performance after one epoch, not training accuracy.

print(f"Test Accuracy: {100 * correct / total:.2f}%")

Test Accuracy: 98.47%

title: Convolutional Neural Network Demo
text:
Connect the Pieces

How do shared convolutional kernels differ from connecting every input pixel to every hidden unit?
Why must the input size of fc1 change if the pooling layout changes?
What happens to prediction variability if dropout is accidentally left in training mode?
Use validation data, not the final test set, when choosing epochs or architecture changes.



Answers and discussion


Convolutions combine locality with shared weights. A 3-by-3 kernel connects to a local patch and reuses the same weights at every spatial position. A dense layer assigns separate weights to each input-to-output connection. Sharing makes a feature detector usable across the image with fewer parameters than an unrestricted dense mapping to the same spatial outputs.
Pooling determines the flattened feature count. Currently the final feature map is 64 x 14 x 14, so fc1 expects 12,544 inputs per image. Adding another 2-by-2, stride-2 pooling stage would reduce it to 64 x 7 x 7, or 3,136 inputs. Both the flattening expression in forward and the input dimension of fc1 must match the new shape; otherwise the tensor operations or batch dimensions will be wrong.
Training-mode dropout makes predictions stochastic. Each forward pass samples a new mask, so repeated predictions for the same image can have different logits and sometimes different labels. model.eval() disables dropout for ordinary evaluation. torch.no_grad() alone does not disable it: gradient tracking and training/evaluation behavior are independent.
Validation supports model selection; testing estimates generalization. Reserve part of the training data for comparing epoch counts, architectures, and other choices. After those choices are fixed, evaluate on the untouched test set. Repeatedly changing the model in response to test accuracy effectively uses the test set for tuning and weakens its role as an independent final check.


Takeaway: a working training pipeline needs consistent shapes, the correct loss inputs, explicit gradient updates, and a separate evaluation mode.

title:

text:
Cheapest, Not Shallowest




Breadth-first search (BFS) minimizes the number of edges.
The direct route S \to G has one edge, but costs 12.

Uniform-cost search (UCS) minimizes the sum of edge costs.
S \to B \to A \to C \to G costs 2+1+1+2=6.



Fewer actions do not necessarily mean a cheaper solution.


Recall the FIFO queue from Lecture 5. Ask which objective BFS optimizes before comparing the two routes. All arrows in this lecture’s worked graph are directed; only the eight drawn edges exist. Reserve about 8 minutes near the end for the existing UCS notebook and allow time for HW1 questions.

(Intro to) AI
text:
UCS Pseudocode: Choose a Node
cost: the popped entry’s stored cost. best[u]: the cheapest cost found so far for u.

  UCS(graph, start, goal)
  best <- default_map(infinity); best[start] <- 0
  parent[start] <- None; Q <- min_priority_queue()
  push(Q, (0, start))
  while Q is not empty:
  (cost, u) <- pop_min(Q)
  if cost != best[u]:  # Skip an obsolete queue entry
  continue
  if u == goal:
  return reconstruct(parent, goal), cost
  RELAX_NEIGHBORS(graph, u, cost, best, parent, Q)
  return failure


Old entry (6, A) still records 6, but best[A] is now 3. Skip the old entry when it is removed.


Explain that best is a dictionary with infinity as its default in an implicit state space; no enumeration of all states is necessary. Parent stores the predecessor for reconstruction. This version inserts a new heap entry on a strict improvement rather than modifying an existing entry. Inserting (3, A) changes best[A] but does not edit or remove the older (6, A) entry. The cheaper entry is removed first; when the older one reaches the front, the cost mismatch identifies it as stale. Nonnegative costs and strict improvements ensure a current entry finalizes its node without needing a separate finalized set. The notebook uses an equally valid visited-on-pop variant instead. The later duplicate-handling slide explains that this particular check is an efficiency guard, not a universal requirement of UCS.

text:
UCS Pseudocode: Improve Its Neighbors
For each outgoing edge u\to v, compare the new route against the stored cost.

  RELAX_NEIGHBORS(graph, u, cost, best, parent, Q)
  for each edge (u, v) with weight w in graph:
  candidate <- cost + w
  if candidate < best[v]:
  best[v] <- candidate
  parent[v] <- u
  push(Q, (candidate, v))


At B: the candidate for A is 2+1=3. Replace best[A] = 6 with 3, set parent[A] = B, and insert (3, A).


The strict comparison avoids reinserting equal-cost routes, including around zero-cost cycles.

title:

(Intro to) AI
text:
Why Cheapest-First Is Optimal
Assume all edge costs are nonnegative. Let the next current entry have cost k.

Every other current frontier entry has cost at least k.
Extending any such route cannot make it cheaper: added cost is at least zero.
Any not-yet-found cheaper route would have a frontier prefix with cost less than k, contradicting the minimum choice.


The node’s cost is final when its current entry is removed. In particular, an accepted goal has optimal cost.


Use induction over finalized nodes. If a cheaper path to u existed, consider its first unfinalized node x. Its finalized predecessor would already have relaxed the edge to x, giving x a frontier entry no more expensive than that path’s prefix. Nonnegative edges bound this prefix below the alleged cheaper total, so x would have been removed before u. Do not claim every discovered cost is optimal.

title:

(Intro to) AI
text:
Negative Edges Break That Argument




The queue first contains G:2 and A:5.
UCS removes the goal at cost 2.

But the route through A costs
5+(-4)=1.
A more expensive prefix can now lead to a cheaper solution.



Nonnegative includes zero. Negative edges require a different shortest-path method, such as Bellman-Ford.


This is a directed acyclic graph, so the issue is not a negative cycle. Bellman-Ford can handle negative edges and detect reachable negative cycles; finite shortest paths require the relevant routes not to benefit from such cycles. Do not turn this into a second algorithm lesson.

section: Completeness Depends on the Search Space
text:
Completeness Depends on the Search Space







Search setting
What ensures UCS eventually finishes?




Finite graph
Nonnegative costs and proper duplicate handling. Zero-cost edges are allowed.


Potentially infinite search space
Finite branching and a positive lower bound c(u,v)\ge\epsilon>0, with a finite-cost goal.



An infinite chain of zero-cost actions could keep UCS busy forever, while a goal with cost 1 waits in the frontier.

Optimality of a returned goal and eventual discovery of a goal are different guarantees.

section: What Does UCS Spend Time On?
text:
What Does UCS Spend Time On?

Exploring many low-cost alternatives before the goal becomes cheapest.
Maintaining a priority queue, rather than a first-in, first-out (FIFO) queue.
Remembering best costs, parents, and pending entries.

For an Explicit Finite Graph
Let V be the number of vertices and E the number of edges. For the duplicate-entry binary heap used in the pseudocode:



Resource
Bound




Time
O\big((V+E)\log(V+E)\big)


Extra storage
O(V+E), including stale heap entries




Assume adjacency lists, nonnegative weights, constant-time dictionary access, and strict improvements. Each node is expanded at most once and each outgoing edge is checked once; each edge can cause at most one insertion during its source’s expansion. An indexed heap with decrease-key and one live entry per vertex instead yields O((V+E) log V) time and O(V) auxiliary storage. Avoid applying the explicit-graph bound to an exponentially large implicit state space.

section: Another Idea: Search from Both Ends
text:
Another Idea: Search from Both Ends


Search forward from the start and backward from the goal.
The backward search generates predecessors: states that can lead to the current state.
A connection gives a candidate route by joining the two paths.


For unit costs, layer-by-layer bidirectional BFS can find a shortest route without searching all the way from one side.


The diagram is a unit-cost chain with undirected edges. Backward BFS traverses the same links; for directed graphs it must reverse the original transitions, not simply follow outgoing edges from the goal. Each side retains parent information for reconstruction. A correct layer-based bidirectional BFS checks intersections between the reached sets while controlling layer order; do not generalize an arbitrary first meeting to weighted search.

When Does Two-Ended Search Help?
With branching factor b and solution depth d, a balanced search suggests:
\underbrace{b^d}_{\text{one direction}}
\quad\text{versus}\quad
\underbrace{2b^{d/2}}_{\text{two directions}}.







Requirement
Why it matters




A known goal, or manageable goal set
The backward search needs a starting point.


Efficient predecessor generation
Reversing actions may be difficult.


Suitable stopping rule
With weights, the first meeting need not be the cheapest route.




The savings are a useful tree-like estimate, not a guarantee for every graph.

text:
Check Your Understanding
A goal enters the queue with cost 20. Can we stop?

No. Another pending route may reach it more cheaply. Test the goal after removing its current entry.

Are zero-cost edges forbidden?

No, not on a finite graph with proper duplicate handling. An infinite zero-cost region can prevent progress toward a positive-cost goal.

If all edges cost 3, will UCS beat BFS in solution cost?

No. Every depth-d route costs 3d, so both minimize the number of edges. Equal-cost routes can differ.

text:
Takeaways

Priority: expand by cumulative path cost g, not depth.
Updates: a discovered node can receive a cheaper route.
Stopping: accept the goal on its current cheapest removal.
Guarantee: nonnegative costs make finalized costs optimal.
Connection: Dijkstra continues the same search for all reachable destinations.


The frontier holds possibilities. Removal, not discovery, certifies the cheapest one.

section: Other Ways to Handle Duplicate Entries
text:
Other Ways to Handle Duplicate Entries
Assume nonnegative edge costs. The exact cost != best[u] check is not required in every UCS implementation.







Method
How repeated work is avoided




Cost check (these slides)
Insert improved entries; skip an entry whose stored cost differs from best[u].


Finalized set (notebook)
On removal, skip a node already finalized; otherwise finalize it and test the goal.


Decrease-key
Keep one pending entry per node and lower its priority on improvement. No obsolete entry remains.




In this pseudocode, strict cost-improvement updates already make stale expansions redundant. Removing the check keeps the correct result, but can waste work.


For UCS, finalize a node on removal, not when it is first discovered.


These are alternatives, not three checks that must all be used together. In the current pseudocode, (3, A) is removed before (6, A), and all outgoing edges of A have already been relaxed using cost 3. Relaxing them again from cost 6 cannot beat the recorded costs, because updates require a strict improvement. Thus skipping the stale entry avoids redundant neighbor scans; omitting this guard does not change the answer under the stated assumptions. This observation is specific to this strict-improvement implementation, not to arbitrary search code. A finalized set is correct with nonnegative costs only when nodes are finalized on removal. Marking A at its first discovery with cost 6 would incorrectly block the route of cost 3. Python’s heapq has no built-in decrease-key operation, which is why inserting a new entry and later skipping duplicates is convenient. The notebook’s visited set implements finalized-on-pop, and its goal test follows the duplicate check.
